findings.summary: Page 1 ends with a process-substitution example five chapters before process substitution is introduced.
findings.evidence: Page 1 code block: "tee >(md5sum > sum.txt) \\", "    >(wc -c > size.txt) > /dev/null", "# several results, one pass over the data" — `>(cmd)` is only defined on page 6 ("`>(cmd)` substitutes a filename that feeds cmd's stdin").
findings.fix: Delete this block from page 1 and keep the `tee >(md5sum ...) >(wc -c ...)` example on page 6, where it already belongs under the fanout material.

findings.summary: The "strict header" is asserted on page 1 with no explanation of any of its flags, which are defined six chapters later.
findings.evidence: Page 1 final code block: "set -euo pipefail", "IFS=$'\\n\\t'   # the strict header" — `set -e`, `set -u` and `pipefail` are first explained on page 7 ("`set -o pipefail` returns the rightmost NON-ZERO status").
findings.fix: Remove the block from page 1; the header already appears in context on page 7's errexit/pipefail material.

findings.summary: The here-string operator `<<<` is used in a worked example on page 3 but only defined on page 4.
findings.evidence: Page 3, heading "One-Line Form" then "read -r a b <<< \"$line\"   # vars survive"; page 4 later states "`<<< \"text\"` is a one-line heredoc" and "Idiomatic field split with no subshell" with no example attached.
findings.fix: Move the `read -r a b <<< "$line"` / `echo "$line" | read a b` code block to page 4, directly under the here-string bullets, so the definition precedes its example and the "idiomatic field split" claim regains its supporting code.

findings.summary: The comment in the "Consumer Quits First" code block is cut off at the right edge, truncating the exit status value.
findings.evidence: Renders as "# yes gets SIGPIPE, status 14" with the final digit clipped; page 7 confirms the value is 141.
findings.fix: Move the comment to its own full-width line or shorten it so "status 141" is fully rendered.

findings.summary: The mechanism of process substitution is explained at the end of page 5 before the construct is named or its syntax shown on page 6.
findings.evidence: Page 5 closing paragraph: "Bash creates a pipe (or FIFO), forks cmd on one end, and passes `/dev/fd/N` of the other end as an ordinary argument." — page 6 only then opens with "`<(cmd)` substitutes a FILENAME that reads cmd's output."
findings.fix: Move that mechanism paragraph to page 6, placing it after the `<(cmd)` / `>(cmd)` definition bullets, and end page 5 with the "A pipe can only feed one thing: stdin" bullets as the lead-in.

findings.summary: The `curl bad-url | tar xz` example claims an exit status of 0, but tar fails on empty/garbage input so the pipeline reports failure, contradicting the point the example is making.
findings.evidence: "curl bad-url | tar xz", "echo $?   # 0 — tar succeeded on empty input"
findings.fix: Replace the last stage with one that genuinely succeeds on empty input, e.g. `curl bad-url | tee out.txt > /dev/null` then `echo $?   # 0 — tee succeeded on empty input`; if tar must stay, annotate the real result (`gzip: stdin: unexpected end of file` / `tar: Child returned status 1`, pipeline status 2).

findings.summary: The "Fanning Out" code block is cut off at its right edge, clipping the closing of the >(logger) redirect.
findings.evidence: Renders as "cmd > >(gzip > out.gz) 2> >(logger" with the closing parenthesis clipped at the dashed border.
findings.fix: Break the command across two lines or reduce the code font size so the complete "2> >(logger)" fits.

findings.summary: Page 6 asserts pipefail behaviour and its function-scoping caveat before `set -o pipefail` is defined on page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 6 bullets: "pipefail flattens detail; `PIPESTATUS` keeps per-stage truth.", "`set -o pipefail` in a function persists after it returns.", "Save and restore, or wrap in `( set -o pipefail; ... )`." — page 7 then introduces it: "`set -o pipefail` returns the rightmost NON-ZERO status."
findings.fix: Cut these three bullets from page 6 (keeping only the `curl bad-url | tar xz` teaser) and place them on page 7 after the pipefail definition and the PIPESTATUS comparison table.

findings.summary: The set -e blind-spot bullets are wrong about `&&`/`||` lists and pipelines: errexit is suppressed only for non-final commands, and a failing final command in either does abort the script.
findings.evidence: "It stays silent in `if`, `while`, `&&`, `||` and `!` contexts." and "It does not catch pipeline failures either."
findings.fix: Restate as: errexit is suppressed only where a status is being tested — an `if`/`while` condition, a `!` negation, and every command in an `&&`/`||` list except the last — so `true && false` and `true | false` DO abort; what it misses is a failure in a non-final pipeline stage (`false | true` stays silent), which is what pipefail fixes.

findings.summary: The second line of the trap code block is cut off at the block's right edge, truncating the word "trap".
findings.evidence: Renders as "set -E   # functions inherit the ERR tr" with the final glyph clipped by the dashed border; the intended text is "the ERR trap".
findings.fix: Shorten the inline comment (e.g. "# functions inherit ERR") or widen/wrap the code block so the full line fits inside the panel.

findings.summary: The "Trusting A Quiet Pipeline" example repeats the false claim that `curl bad | tar xz` exits 0.
findings.evidence: "curl bad | tar xz; echo $?  # 0"
findings.fix: Use a genuinely-succeeding final stage (`curl bad | tee out.txt > /dev/null; echo $?  # 0`, or `curl bad | wc -l`) so the demonstration of a lying pipeline status is actually true, and keep the `set -o pipefail` / `PIPESTATUS` lines beneath it.

findings.summary: The "Leaks And Races" heading is the last block on page 9 with its bullets stranded on page 10.
findings.evidence: Page 9 final block: {"type":"heading","text":"Leaks And Races"}; page 10 opens with "Unclosed `exec 3<` leaks fds; long loops hit `EMFILE`.", "`>(cmd)` output may be incomplete when the script exits.", "Add `wait` before you read what the writer produced."
findings.fix: Move the heading onto page 10 so it sits directly above its three bullets, or pull the bullet block back onto page 9 under the heading.

findings.summary: The PIPESTATUS code block's second line is cut off at the block's right edge, truncating the comment.
findings.evidence: Renders as 'st=("${PIPESTATUS[@]}")   # next l' with the last characters clipped at the dashed border; intended "# next line".
findings.fix: Shorten the comment to "# copy now" or allow the code block to wrap so the full comment is visible.

findings.summary: The operator table defines `>|` by reference to noclobber before noclobber is introduced later on the same page.
findings.evidence: Table row ["`>| file`","force past noclobber","fd 1"] appears several blocks above the heading "noclobber Guard" and "set -o noclobber".
findings.fix: Either move the `>| file` row into the noclobber section, or move the "noclobber Guard" code block above the operator table.

findings.summary: `/dev/tcp` and `/dev/udp` are labelled Bash-only although the feature originated in ksh93 and ksh supports it.
findings.evidence: "Bash-only: `> /dev/tcp/host/port` and `/dev/udp/...` open sockets."
findings.fix: Change to "Bash and ksh93 only (not POSIX; absent in dash/zsh): `> /dev/tcp/host/port` …".

findings.summary: A heredoc terminator with trailing whitespace does not normally produce `unexpected end of file`; Bash emits a here-document warning and silently swallows the rest of the file.
findings.evidence: "One stray space and Bash reports `unexpected end of file`." (repeated on the last page as "Trailing whitespace after the terminator: `unexpected end of file`.")
findings.fix: State the actual diagnostic: `bash: warning: here-document at line N delimited by end-of-file (wanted 'EOF')` — and note that the remaining script lines are consumed as heredoc body, with `syntax error: unexpected end of file` appearing only when the unterminated heredoc leaves a compound command (function, `if`, loop) open.

findings.summary: A heredoc example is left syntactically incomplete, appended to an unrelated finished example in the same block.
findings.evidence: Page 4 code block: "cat <<EOF > out.txt", "line one", "EOF", "cat 3<<EOF   # block lands on fd 3, not stdin" — the fd-3 heredoc has no body and no terminator.
findings.fix: Split it into its own block with a complete example, e.g. `cat <<EOF 3<<'X'`-free form: "cat 3<<EOF", "payload line", "EOF" with a comment noting the block lands on fd 3.

findings.summary: `sort -m` is cited as a consumer that re-reads or seeks its input, but it is a pure streaming merge and works fine on a process-substitution pipe.
findings.evidence: "`sort -m` or `tar` on tape can need a re-read and break."
findings.fix: Drop `sort -m` and use consumers that genuinely need `lseek`, e.g. "`unzip`, `ffprobe` on some containers, or `tar -r`/`-u` need to seek and fail on `/dev/fd/63`."

findings.summary: The comment under the diff example is cut off at the code block's right edge.
findings.evidence: Renders as "# two live outputs, zero temp file" with the trailing "s" clipped by the dashed border.
findings.fix: Shorten the comment to "# two live outputs, no temp files" or widen the block.

findings.summary: The yellow sticky note and its pin overlap the last line of the "Trusting A Quiet Pipeline" code block.
findings.evidence: The pin graphic sits on top of the text 'st=("${PIPESTATUS[@]}")   # next line', partially obscuring the word "next".
findings.fix: Shift the sticky note down and right so it clears the code block's text baseline, or anchor it outside the code panel.

findings.summary: Page 9 opens with repairs before the mistakes they repair are stated, including `sort -o`, which has not yet appeared.
findings.evidence: First bullets: "`sort f > tmp && mv tmp f` works for tools without `-o`." and "Two opens make two independent offsets that overwrite." — the mistakes table ("`sort f > f` | file emptied | `sort -o f f`", "`> f 2> f` | streams clash") comes after them.
findings.fix: Put the Written/Result/Repair table first and demote the bullets to commentary beneath it, so each fix follows the mistake it addresses.
